claim: A small but significant fraction of PV interneuron spikes occurred during down states.

claim: The firing of both SST and PV interneurons during up states may causally contribute to their ending.
source: Altogether, these findings led us to hypothesize that the firing of both SST and PV interneurons during up states may causally contribute to their ending, whereas the firing of interneurons during down state, at least for PV cells, may delay the transition from the down state to the up state.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the phase locking and phase speed analysis.

claim: The firing of interneurons during down state, at least for PV cells, may delay the transition from the down state to the up state.

claim: A brief light stimulus applied during an ongoing up state generated a pronounced and long-lasting hyperpolarization in layer II/III principal neurons in PV-Cre mice.
source: Using patch-clamp recording from layer II/III principal neurons in injected PV-Cre and SST-Cre mice under anaesthesia (Figure 3), we found that a brief (duration: 10 ms) light stimulus applied during an ongoing up state generated a pronounced and long-lasting hyperpolarization which outlasted the light stimulus and resembled a transition to a down state (Figure 3a–c, left panel, Figure 3f–h, left panel)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a-c, left panel.

claim: Photoactivation of PV cells during an ongoing up state resulted in a sudden decrease in the power of high-frequency oscillations in the LFP.

claim: The effect of optogenetic activation of PV interneurons during an ongoing up state was similar in awake, head-restrained mice compared to anesthetized mice.
source: We then performed patch-clamp recordings in awake, head-restrained mice during quiet wakefulness. Under these experimental conditions cortical activities were characterized by frequent transitions between the up and the down states in accordance with previous reports (Petersen et al., 2003b). Importantly, we found (Figure 3c,h right panels and Figure 3—figure supplement 6) that the effect of optogenetic activation of PV and SST interneurons during an ongoing up state was similar to that observed in anesthetized mice, ruling out any possible side effect of anaesthesia.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3c, right panel and Figure 3—figure supplement 6, and citation to previous work (Petersen et al., 2003b).

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of PV cells during an ongoing down state triggered a membrane depolarization in pyramidal cells in anesthetized mice.
source: To test this hypothesis we inhibited PV and SST cells during ongoing down states. We found that individual principal cells and the cortical network reliably transitioned to an active state, which resembled an up state, upon photoinhibition of interneurons. Optogenetic inhibition of PV and SST cells during an ongoing down state triggered a membrane depolarization in pyramidal cells in anesthetized and non-anesthetized mice (Figure 4d,e,i,j and Figure 4—figure supplement 2c,f) which could overlast the light stimulus.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4d,e.

claim: Inhibiting PV interneurons facilitated down-to-up transitions with less jitter compared to the inhibition of SST cells in anesthetized mice.

evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (p = 6E-4).

claim: Photoinhibition of PV cells triggered down-to-up transitions with larger slope compared to spontaneous transitions.

claim: Local activation of PV interneurons in one cortical region during an up state causes a transition to the down state that occurs near synchronously in both recorded areas located ~2 mm apart.
source: Using simultaneous recordings of network and single cell activity in two brain regions located ~2 mm apart, we demonstrated that local activation of interneurons in one of the two regions during an up state causes a transition to the down state that occurs near synchronously in both recorded areas (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Photo-inhibition of PV interneurons during an ongoing down state reliably triggered a transition to the up state in two recorded areas located >2 mm apart.
source: Moreover, our data also show that photo-inhibition of interneurons during an ongoing up state significantly affects network activity at distal cortical locations. When interneurons were locally inhibited in one region during a down state a transition to the up state was reliably observed in two recorded areas located >2 mm apart (Figure 6e,f,k,l), directly demonstrating a role of local inhibition in the control of down state synchrony across cortical areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6e,f.

claim: The weak firing activity of interneurons during cortical down state is fundamental to maintain the cortical circuitry in the silent state, preventing it from escaping into the up state.
source: Based on these results, we propose that the weak firing activity of interneurons during cortical down state is fundamental to maintain the cortical circuitry in the silent state, preventing it from escaping into the up state.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the optogenetic inhibition experiments showing that inhibiting interneurons during down states triggers up states.

claim: During quiet wakefulness or NREM sleep the cortex displays rhythmic electrical signals characterized by large-amplitude and low frequency (<1 Hz) oscillations.
source: For example, during quiet wakefulness or NREM sleep the cortex and other brain regions (e.g., the thalamus) display rhythmic electrical signals characterized by large-amplitude and low frequency (<1 Hz) oscillations (Metherate et al., 1992; Steriade et al., 1993a; Crunelli and Hughes, 2010; Halassa et al., 2014; Slézia et al., 2011; Fogerson and Huguenard, 2016; Herrera et al., 2016; Sellers et al., 2015).

claim: Slow oscillations are dominated by recurring transitions between active (up) and silent (down) periods.

evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about slow oscillations.

claim: In the cortex, up states are associated with sustained membrane potential depolarization in single pyramidal neurons and enhanced firing at the network level.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Steriade et al., 1993b; Contreras and Steriade, 1995; Vyazovskiy et al., 2009).
